Some of these uprisings had a social, and even a class, character. Examples include the revolt of enslaved people in Syria at an earlier stage (al-Masʿūdī, Meadows of Gold, vol. 3), the revolt in Basra during the time of al-Ḥajjāj (al-Balādhurī, Ansāb al-Ashrāf, p. 303), and the uprisings of poor commoners and Turkic peasants in Central Asia in 73 AH.↩︎

After the killing of ʿUthmān, the political split into two main camps—supporters of the Umayyads and their opponents—was reflected in legal and theological thought. Jurists and theologians disagreed over a basic question: must people patiently endure the injustice of an oppressive ruler, or must they resist him? The Imamis, Muʿtazilites, and Khārijites held that such a ruler had to be opposed and resisted. See Shaykh Muḥammad Jawād Mughniyya, Landmarks of Islamic Philosophy, Beirut, 1960, p. 21. The Sunnis, by contrast, held that ideally the imam should be virtuous, just, and benevolent; but if he was not, patient obedience to an unjust ruler was preferable to rebelling against him. See the same source, quoting Shaykh Abū Zahra, Islamic Schools.↩︎

We can see this in the different names given to these theological discussions before kalām became an independent discipline. They were sometimes called “the principles of religion” (uṣūl al-dīn), sometimes “understanding religion” (al-fiqh fī al-dīn). Abū Ḥanīfa (d. 150 AH/767 CE) called them “the greater jurisprudence” (al-fiqh al-akbar). They were also called “the science of divine unity,” “the science of divine unity and attributes,” and “the science of religious laws and rulings.” See al-Tahānawī, Kashshāf Iṣṭilāḥāt al-Funūn.↩︎

There are several views about why the discipline came to be called ʿilm al-kalām. Al-Nasafī, for example, says in al-ʿAqāʾid al-Nasafiyya, pp. 10–11, that it was called kalām because, like logic and philosophy, it gives a person the ability to speak effectively in establishing religious doctrines and compelling opponents to accept the argument. Al-Shahrastānī gives another explanation in al-Milal, vol. 1, p. 33, printed in the margin of Ibn Ḥazm’s al-Fiṣal. He says that after leading Muʿtazilites studied the philosophers’ books “when they were translated in the days of al-Maʾmūn, they mixed the philosophers’ methods with those of kalām, made it a separate branch of knowledge, and called it kalām. This may have been because the most prominent question they discussed and fought over was the question of the kalām [speech] of God, so the whole discipline was named after it. Or it may have been because they were answering the philosophers, who called one branch of their knowledge manṭiq [logic]. Manṭiq and kalām can both mean speech.”↩︎

Historians of the period before the great flourishing of authorship under the Abbasids mention many writers and books from that earlier time. For example, al-Maqrīzī (al-Khiṭaṭ, vol. 2, p. 345) says that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ wrote a book titled The Intermediate Position. They also mention a book by the Muʿtazilite ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd refuting those who upheld predestination, as well as works by Imami, Khārijite, and other theologians. See Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, Introduction to the History of Islamic Philosophy, p. 288.↩︎

Claude Cahen explains the relationship between al-Maʾmūn and the Muʿtazilites in two ways. First, Hārūn al-Rashīd distrusted the Muʿtazilites, and al-Amīn did the same, so it was natural for the Muʿtazilites to side with al-Maʾmūn. Second, Cahen argues that al-Maʾmūn’s support for the Muʿtazilites was implicitly an attempt to win over the Zaydis, who were among the strongest followers of Muʿtazilism. See Claude Cahen, History of the Arabs and the Islamic Peoples, Beirut, 1972, vol. 1, p. 110. This explanation has a basis in reality, but it stays at the surface of the phenomenon and does not take account of the more powerful social factor.↩︎

Al-Mutawakkil was not “the first Abbasid caliph to love luxury.” Luxury had already accompanied the lives of Abbasid caliphs before him, just as it had accompanied the Umayyad caliphs before them. This was natural: it was an objective social phenomenon, though there were differences and exceptions, such as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and al-Manṣūr. What distinguished al-Mutawakkil was that his love of luxury was more extravagant and excessive than that of others.↩︎
